subject: research/selfrep-extinction-kits
professional: an applied probabilist working on stochastic population dynamics and demographic extinction (birth-death chains, branching-process establishment probabilities, quasi-stationary distributions: the Kendall / Nasell / Haccou-Jagers-Vatutin tradition). First checks: is the CTMC generator right (births, retirements, kit grabbing, truncation), are the absorption probability and mean absorption time solved correctly and insensitive to truncation, is the first-generation bound a valid closed form and a true lower bound, does the 'early extinction' threshold drive the answer, and is the work positioned against the establishment-probability literature

evidence.verification: python3 -m unittest discover -s tests: 7 tests OK. Six seeded mutations via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: three caught (build rate b/w -> b/(1.5w), idle retirement rate halved, builder retirement leaving an idle machine), three SURVIVED: first_generation_extinction dropping the build-race factor (the headline 0.162 becomes 0.078; tests check only the two limits and p_chain > gen1, which a smaller gen1 still satisfies), the lognormal build-time location sign flipped (mean build time 50 h -> 52 h), and the Weibull scale losing its Gamma(1+1/k) correction (mean life no longer L). The chain's generator is well covered through the chain-vs-simulation test; the closed form and the DES's non-Markov switches, which carry Sections B and C's 'regular/logn' columns, are not. A seventh mutant (Gauss-Seidel tolerance -> 1e-3 absolute) was dropped as near-equivalent: it moves the L=300 mean time by 0.2 h.
evidence.craft: Read src/selfrep_extinction_kits/chain.py (97 lines), des.py (72), tests/test_extinction_kits.py, experiments/run.py and figure.py. Small, readable, docstrings state the assumptions and the state invariant i*k == 0; truncation is explicit and checked. Minor: Gauss-Seidel in pure Python where a sparse direct solve would be exact and simpler; redundant list comprehension at chain.py:53; kit stock silently clipped at kmax (documented as truncation); DES idle machines held in a list with O(n) remove; run.py is a top-level script with no main(); figure.py imports research/_shared/linefig, not listed under 'Outside dependencies'. No dead code or copied engines.
evidence.claims: Checked against results.txt: chain 0.194 vs sim 0.198 +- 0.006 (backed); 'agree within about two standard errors' across seven cases (largest gap 1.1 SE in A, 1.7 SE in C; backed); gen1 0.162 and 0.047 at L=2000 (backed); 'shift by at most about 0.04 (0.297 vs 0.335)' (0.038, backed); Weibull 0.194/0.028/0.004/0.000 (backed); mean times 117/201/1464/10994 vs sim 112+-3/196+-6/1511+-50/10625+-325 (backed); 'about double' 23460 vs 10995 and 26173 vs 13257 (backed; README quotes 10995 while the table shows 10994 at 20/8 and 10996 at 30/12, trivial); comparisons to selfrep-wearout (20% dead at L=500, 3% at 2000, unchanged with recycling, seed fleets did not help at L=200) all match research/selfrep-wearout/README.md:24-27. Not quite backed: the research homepage summary (research/_homepage/projects.json:2145) says relaxing the Markov assumptions moves the probability 'by at most about 0.03'; the table's largest shift is 0.038 (the README's 0.04 is right). Stale: README:7 says the two companion chains were not reconciled; research/selfrep-reconcile now does that, and two of the README:41 next steps (seed fleets n0 > 1, quasi-stationary approximation) were done in research/selfrep-extinction-qsd; neither is linked. 'Stylised', 'assumed inputs', 'simulated only' and the AI-assistance note are present; limitations are honest (threshold choice, truncation, comparison to selfrep-wearout by reading).
evidence.fitness: A researcher can and did build on it: selfrep-extinction-qsd and selfrep-reconcile import its chain. Nearest prior work: the probability that a small founding population is lost before it establishes, and the mean time to extinction of a density-limited birth-death chain, are classical (Kendall 1948, 'On the generalized birth-and-death process', Ann. Math. Stat. 19:1-15; Haccou, Jagers & Vatutin 2005, 'Branching Processes: Variation, Growth, and Extinction of Populations', Cambridge; Nasell 2001, 'Extinction and quasi-stationarity in the Verhulst logistic model', J. Theor. Biol. 211:11-27; Lande, Engen & Saether 2003, 'Stochastic Population Dynamics in Ecology and Conservation', OUP). The README says the method is textbook and cites none of this; the contribution is a correct, honestly scoped application of that theory to the repository's own stylised printer shop, explaining a sibling project's simulation. Sound, but not a new or publishable result at the research/CLAUDE.md PhD bar; no branching-process (establishment-probability) approximation is compared, and the 'early extinction' threshold of 6 is not varied (my check: 0.185/0.191/0.194/0.196/0.198 for thresholds 3/4/6/10/15, so the result is robust below the 11.7-machine equilibrium; the project did not show this).
evidence.domain: The method is standard practice and is applied correctly: absorption probabilities and expected absorption times of a finite CTMC, solved to tolerance and checked against a larger truncation (my dense solves agree to 4 decimals), a valid closed-form lower bound from memoryless races, and a DES that relaxes one assumption at a time. A population-dynamics probabilist would sign off on the mechanics with the stated limits; they would ask for the threshold sensitivity, a branching-process establishment approximation as the analytic baseline, and the classical citations.

defects.what: The closed-form first-generation bound (the headline 0.162) and the DES's non-Markov switches are untested: dropping the build-race factor (0.162 -> 0.078), flipping the lognormal location sign, or removing the Weibull Gamma(1+1/k) scale correction all leave the 7 tests green. Tests check only the bound's two limits and p_chain > gen1, so Sections B and the 'regular/logn' columns rest on unchecked parametrisations.

Nearest prior work not cited: establishment probability of a small founding population and mean extinction time of density-limited birth-death chains are classical (Kendall 1948; Nasell 2001; Lande, Engen & Saether 2003; Haccou, Jagers & Vatutin 2005). The README says it cites none; there is no branching-process establishment approximation as an analytic baseline and the early-extinction threshold is not varied. A correct application, not a new result at the research/CLAUDE.md PhD bar.

verdict: selfrep-extinction-kits' numbers are right: run.py reproduces results.txt byte-for-byte, and an independent numpy generator-matrix solve (own state space, dense solve, not Gauss-Seidel) matches every early-extinction probability (0.1944 at L=500, B=4) and every mean extinction time (1464.6 h at L=200) to the printed digits, stable at larger truncations; the closed-form bound (0.1623) and an independent Gillespie run (0.1968 +- 0.0028) agree, and a hand Weibull calculation confirms the wear-out mechanism. It misses the bar on verification: 3 of 6 seeded bugs survive, including one that halves the headline first-generation bound. As research it is a sound, honestly scoped application of textbook birth-death theory that explains a sibling simulation and has been built on, but it cites none of the establishment-probability literature and is not a new result at the PhD bar.
